doc.title: Jon Hendricks — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Al Jarreau at the Trident and teaching singers to sing the chords
summary: Al Jarreau watched him nightly and learned his advice to know the melody and sing the chords.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: It seems as though you attracted many other artists there too . . .
Al Jarreau used to come in every night. I saw this handsome guy who reminded me of myself.

He looked like me. I said, “Look at this guy.” He was tall and a very, very handsome cat. He was looking at me almost like examining something under a microscope. He was watching me, almost clinically watching me, everything I did. So I started to talk to him. I says, “What do you do?” He says, “I want to be a singer.” He says . . .
You sounded just like him at that point.

Yeah. He says, “I would like to be a jazz singer.” I said, “Oh. Why don’t you come up and sing something.” He says, “Oh, no, no, no, no. Not with you. Not with you.” I said, “Come on.” So I got him up, and he sang a tune. Then he asked me – he says, “How do you scat?” I’ve had people ask me that a lot. I had evolved my answer, which we talked about yesterday. I told him, “You know the melody.” He says, “Yeah.” I said, “Sing the chords.” Out of all the singers I had told this to, only two really picked up on it and did it. One was Al Jarreau. The other was Jack Jones. Jack Jones can scat. He took that idea right into John Coltrane, whom he also loved. Judith: George can [?] too.
George could do it because he played. So he could do it anyway. But I’m talking about singers that didn’t know how to do it. George always could scat.
